AI · 75 pts

### Adapter Cartel

A single adapter on a shared model hub passed review cleanly, and so did every one of the eight adapters in this hub, checked one at a time. The scanner still flagged the collection as a whole without saying why, which was the entire puzzle: no individual member looked guilty.

A low rank adapter does not store new weights, only two small matrices whose product gets added to a base weight when the adapter is merged. Stack several adapters and their contributions add. Reading the configs showed four of the eight adapters targeted an unusual extra weight in the base model that the other four never touched. Each of those four updates on its own was a full matrix of noisy looking values that would pass any single review. Summed together, the negative components cancelled and every remaining value landed on a small whole number, and reading that merged matrix as bytes spelled the flag. ## Cloud

1 solve · 76 points · four flags in one chain

Cloud · 76 pts

### Deputy

A low privilege analyst key into a partner cloud account was the starting point, and the prompt’s own advice, read your own policy before doing anything else, turned out to be the whole method for the first flag. The analyst could read its own permissions freely, and those permissions granted narrow storage access plus the ability to pass one specific role to a new serverless function and invoke it.

That combination is a well known escalation path. The analyst could not assume the privileged role directly, since its trust policy only allowed the serverless service itself to assume it, but creating a function that runs as that role and then invoking it hands back that role’s own live credentials. Acting as that more privileged role opened a cross account trust relationship into a partner account’s administrative role, and that assumption succeeded with no additional secret required at all, because the partner account trusted anything holding the right permission on the caller’s side without checking who was really behind it.

The final and sharpest lesson sat inside that administrative role’s own storage: a configuration file naming a second, supposedly hardened role and the shared secret needed to assume it, stored right next to the door it was meant to protect and readable by the very role that secret was guarding against. Assuming that hardened role with its own leaked secret reached the last vault.

#### Takeaway

Every individual control in this chain was a real, correctly implemented cloud permission check. None of them failed on its own. What failed was the assumption that a secret is safe once it sits one door further in, when the account granting that door already had read access to it.

## Crypto

3 solves · 1,083 points

Crypto · 63 pts

### Owner’s Draw

A payment webhook signed its requests with a hash of a secret concatenated with the request body, labelled plainly as such by the service itself. That specific construction, a bare hash over a secret followed by an attacker visible message rather than a proper keyed hash, carries a well known weakness: the hash’s output is exactly the algorithm’s internal state after processing that input, so anyone holding a valid message and its digest can resume the computation and extend the message with anything they like, computing a valid digest for the extended message without ever learning the secret.

Several natural guesses at that function were tried and ruled out quickly, including a fixed step, a fixed ratio, and each value depending only on public parts of the previous signature. The one that fit was a general linear relation with two unknown constants tying each secret value to the next. Each signature also gives an equation relating its own secret value to the unknown private key through publicly known numbers, so substituting one relation into the other produces, after treating one product of two unknowns as a fourth unknown to keep everything linear, one straightforward equation in four unknowns for every consecutive pair of signatures. A handful of consecutive signatures gave enough equations to solve the whole system exactly, no guessing or heavy search required, and checking the recovered private key against the published public key confirmed the solve before it was used. With the key in hand, signing the previously refused transaction and submitting it was immediate.

#### Takeaway

A deterministic sequence of secret values is only as safe as the difficulty of learning the rule connecting them, and a general linear relation is often solvable exactly with plain algebra once it is correctly identified, no brute force needed.

## Forensics

3 solves · 202 points

Forensics · 63 pts

### Gone Not Forgotten

A messaging app insisted a suspect’s device held nothing incriminating, and the message table on the phone backed that up, showing a small run of ordinary numbered rows with one number conspicuously missing from the sequence. A missing row number in a database table with no larger context does not by itself mean a message is truly gone.

A database of this kind, when it deletes a row, does not typically erase the underlying bytes; it only removes the row’s reference and marks that space free for reuse. Until something else happens to reuse that space, the deleted row’s raw content still sits inside the file. The app also obfuscated every stored message body with a fixed, simple keyed transform, described plainly in an accompanying configuration note. Scanning the raw database file directly for runs of data in the stored encoding, rather than trusting the table’s own view of its rows, and reversing that same transform on every candidate run recovered several message bodies including the one that had been deleted, which decoded cleanly to the flag while the surviving decoy candidates decoded to garbage.

#### Takeaway

A record removed from an index is not the same as a record removed from storage, and any format that reuses freed space lazily rather than immediately will keep evidence around for exactly as long as nothing has overwritten it.

Forensics · 63 pts

### Ghost in the Timeline

An engineer’s alibi rested on three claims about a disputed file: that it existed before their access began, that every timestamp on it agreed, and that nothing had been staged or deleted. Filesystem metadata usually carries more than one kind of timestamp, and not every kind is equally easy to fake.

The file’s modification time did indeed sit safely in the past, matching the alibi. Its creation time, a separate field some filesystems keep that ordinary timestamp editing tools do not normally touch, told a very different and much more recent story, directly contradicting the alibi and lining up with when a neighbouring, honestly dated file was created. The third claim broke on closer inspection of the filesystem’s own record of deleted files, which still listed a zip archive under a caching folder even though the visible directory only showed a dangling reference to it, and a login log corroborated exactly when it had been created and by whom. Recovering that deleted archive’s content directly from the filesystem’s low level tools produced a small file inside it holding the flag.

#### Takeaway

Trust the timestamp an attacker cannot easily reach over the ones they can. Ordinary tools that backdate a file rewrite the timestamps meant for humans to read, but rarely touch the one meant to record true creation.

Forensics · 76 pts

### Deep Freeze

Responders reached a ransomware infected workstation while the malware was still actively encrypting files, and rather than letting the machine power down cleanly they captured its memory on the spot, mid attack. The prompt’s own framing said as much: catching a thief mid reach means they are still holding what they took.

That framing turned out to be the entire solve. Rather than reconstructing the ransomware’s key from a partial encrypted file, a plain search for the flag’s known text pattern across the raw memory capture found it sitting in the clear twice over: once as an environment variable the running ransomware process had been launched with, and once inside the still resident plaintext of the very document it had been in the middle of encrypting when the machine was frozen. A convincing decoy value existed too, matching a script’s own hardcoded fallback default rather than anything actually assigned for this run.

#### Takeaway

Memory captured while a process is still running holds far more in the clear than anyone analysing only its disk footprint would expect, and a search over raw memory is always worth trying before reaching for a heavier reconstruction.

## Hardware

5 solves · 1,281 points

Hardware · 181 pts

### Afterglow

A salvaged departure board’s flash image booted into a small program that painted the same fixed demo banner on every unit and waited at a keypad for a numeric service code that was never shown on screen anywhere. The real per unit information had to be read off the panel by entering the correct code first.

Disassembling the boot image as sixteen bit real mode code showed the keypad routine comparing whatever was typed against a value computed at boot from a short, per instance value baked directly into the image, run through two rounds of a simple integer mixing function. Because that mixing function and the seed value were both fully readable from the image file itself, the correct code could be computed entirely offline with no need to interact with the running board first. Typing that computed code caused the board to decrypt its own stored demo banner data using a keystream derived from that same service code, revealing that the shared decoy image had secretly been doubling as ciphertext the entire time.

#### Takeaway

Notice when supposedly meaningless shared data is unusually large or oddly placed for what it claims to be. A banner that looks identical across every unit is a natural place to also hide unit specific ciphertext.

FlagH7CTF{...}

Hardware · 63 pts

### Radio Silence

A single unlabelled radio burst, captured once and never repeated, needed to be read back with no protocol documentation at all. The raw capture’s amplitude stayed almost perfectly constant across its active portion, which ruled out any scheme that encodes information in signal strength and pointed toward frequency or phase instead.

Measuring the instantaneous frequency across the burst showed it sitting almost entirely at two distinct values, each held for a short, consistent duration before switching, the textbook shape of a two level frequency shift keyed signal at a fixed symbol rate. An initial pass smoothed the frequency estimate too aggressively and appeared to show a third, intermediate frequency that turned out to be nothing more than an averaging artifact from blending two adjacent symbols together; sampling each symbol’s own short window individually resolved cleanly into only the two real levels. Mapping the lower frequency to one bit value and the higher to the other produced a clean bit stream opening with a long alternating preamble, followed directly by the flag in plain text.

#### Takeaway

A constant envelope signal is telling you where not to look. When amplitude carries nothing, check frequency and phase before assuming a more complex scheme, and always sample each symbol on its own terms rather than averaging across symbol boundaries.

### Open Sesame

A cheap garage remote advertised a brand new, unguessable code on every button press, and eight consecutive presses were captured to test that claim. The prompt’s own distinction, that unguessable and unpredictable are different properties. There was a pattern that was revealed.

The capture’s amplitude pattern was cleanly two level with a fixed total period per bit, the signature of a simple duty cycle encoded scheme rather than anything more elaborate. Splitting the capture into its eight separate transmissions and comparing them bit by bit showed most of each frame was an identical fixed device identifier, followed by a short field that simply counted upward by the same fixed step on every single press, followed by one last short field that cycled through only a handful of distinct values in a short repeating pattern tied to the press count. ## Pwn

1 solve · 884 points

Pwn · 884 pts

### Frame of Reference

One such object was freed immediately after starting a coroutine that still held a live reference into it. Because the pool reused freed space in strict order, allocating a different, unrelated object next guaranteed it landed at that same freed address. When the coroutine resumed, it read the unrelated object’s bytes as the original key material, and a stray pointer from that object leaked out through an ordinary looking numeric result the service printed. A fixed offset in the program’s own binary connected that leaked pointer straight to a privileged function’s address.

A second round of the same setup made a value the service would normally just compute come out equal to that target address, overwriting a second object’s internal pointer with it. Calling that object’s ordinary functionality then jumped straight into the privileged function, which printed the flag.

Section 8

## Key Lessons

What carried across categories

### The review unit and the trust unit are often not the same thing

Adapter Cartel and Deputy both broke a system that reviewed its parts correctly in isolation. A backdoor split across several low rank adapters, or a secret trusted one door further in than it should have been, only shows up once you review the combination, not the pieces.

### A guard only protects the representation it actually inspects

Dog Whistle’s safety check scanned the audible band while an analog nonlinearity smuggled a command in through ultrasonic tones that mixed down after the check ran. Anything downstream of an inspection point needs its own defence.

### Deleted rarely means erased

Gone Not Forgotten and Ghost in the Timeline both turned on the same fact from two different angles: a database that reuses freed space lazily, and a filesystem whose deletion bookkeeping outlives the directory entry, both keep evidence around long after a human would call it gone.

### A container format’s index is a convenience, not the whole truth

Overexposed’s flag sat across a PNG text chunk and two ZIP local headers that no directory ever listed. A summary index tells you what its author wanted you to see, not everything that is actually there.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Network

There are two different ways to connect to the competition network: Vulnbox and player VPN. The first is based on WireGuard, the second is based on OpenVPN. When the VPNs are online, you will find VPN configs containing the required secrets in the Downloads page of your team. We will generate new configs once a day, so you might have to wait some hours.

### Vulnbox VPN

Connecting to this VPN is required. It provides access to the competition network for your Vulnbox, and optionally also your team.

We offer two options for connecting the Vulnbox VM to the Vulnbox VPN. The one to use is selected when booting the Vulnbox for the first time:

  * Separate router machine: The VPN runs on a router box under your responsibility. This might be another VM, the box which hosts the hypervisor, or a completely different machine. The Vulnbox sets its IP statically and sends its traffic to the competition network through the router machine. This will allow you to use the remaining addresses from the Vulnbox network for connecting other machines through the same router, e.g. individual team members when playing on-site.
